subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: \(\triangle DEF \sim \triangle MNK\). If \(DE = 5\), \(MN = 6\), then find the value of \(\dfrac{A(\triangle DEF)}{A(\triangle MNK)}\).
solution: By the theorem of areas of similar triangles, \(\dfrac{A(\triangle DEF)}{A(\triangle MNK)} = \dfrac{DE^{2}}{MN^{2}} = \dfrac{5^{2}}{6^{2}} = \dfrac{25}{36}\).

stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle B = 90^\circ\), \(\angle C = 60^\circ\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\) and \(AC = 18\). Find \(BC\).
solution: \(\triangle ABC\) is a \(30^\circ\text{-}60^\circ\text{-}90^\circ\) triangle and \(BC\) is the side opposite to \(30^\circ\). \(\therefore BC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{hypotenuse} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times AC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 = 9\) cm.
figureNote: right-angled triangle ABC, right angle at B, angle A = 30 deg, angle C = 60 deg, hypotenuse AC = 18 cm, p-00

stem: In the figure, line \(SR\) is a tangent to the circle at \(Q\) and \(m(\text{arc } PMQ) = 130^\circ\). Find \(\angle PQS\).
solution: By the tangent-secant (tangent-chord) angle theorem, \(\angle PQS = \dfrac{1}{2} \times m(\text{arc } PMQ) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 130^\circ = 65^\circ\).
figureNote: circle with chord PQ and a tangent line through S-Q-R touching at Q, point M on arc PQ, p-00

stem: If the angle \(\theta = -60^\circ\), find the value of \(\cos\theta\).
solution: \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\). \(\therefore \cos(-60^\circ) = \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

stem: Find the slope of the line with inclination \(30^\circ\).
solution: Slope \(= \tan\theta = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Thus, the slope of the line is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

stem: Using Euler's formula, find \(V\) if \(E = 30\), \(F = 12\).
solution: Euler's formula: \(F + V = E + 2\). \(\therefore 12 + V = 30 + 2 = 32\). \(\therefore V = 32 - 12 = 20\).

subtopic: Property of an Angle Bisector of a Triangle
stem: In \(\triangle PQR\), seg \(RS\) is the bisector of \(\angle PRQ\). If \(PS = 6\), \(SQ = 8\), \(PR = 15\), find \(QR\).
solution: By the angle bisector property, \(\dfrac{PR}{QR} = \dfrac{PS}{SQ}\). \(\therefore \dfrac{15}{QR} = \dfrac{6}{8}\). \(\therefore QR = \dfrac{15 \times 8}{6} = 20\).
figureNote: triangle PQR with S on side PQ and cevian RS; PS = 6, SQ = 8, PR = 15, p-01

stem: In the figure, a tangent segment \(PA\) touching a circle at \(A\) and a secant \(PBC\) is shown. If \(AP = 15\), \(BP = 10\), find \(BC\).
solution: \(PA\) is a tangent segment and \(PBC\) is the secant. \(\therefore PB \times PC = PA^{2}\). \(\therefore 10 \times PC = 15^{2}\). \(\therefore PC = \dfrac{225}{10} = 22.5\). Now, \(PB + BC = PC\) (\(P\text{-}B\text{-}C\)). \(\therefore 10 + BC = 22.5\). \(\therefore BC = 22.5 - 10 = 12.5\).
figureNote: circle with tangent segment PA at A and secant from external point P cutting the circle at B and C; AP = 15, BP = 10, p-01

stem: Draw an equilateral \(\triangle ABC\) with side \(6.2\) cm and construct its circumcircle.
solution: Steps of construction: (1) Construct the equilateral \(\triangle ABC\) of side \(6.2\) cm. (2) Draw the perpendicular bisectors of any two sides. (3) Mark their point of intersection as \(O\) (the circumcentre). (4) Draw a circle with centre \(O\) and radius \(OA\) (\(= OB = OC\)). This is the required circumcircle.

stem: For the angle in standard position, if the initial arm rotates \(25^\circ\) in the anticlockwise direction, then state the quadrant in which the terminal arm lies. (Draw the figure and write the answer.)
solution: The initial arm rotates \(25^\circ\) in the anticlockwise direction, so the angle is positive and its measure lies between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\). Thus, the terminal arm lies in quadrant I.

subtopic: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
stem: Find the area of a sector whose arc length and radius are \(10\) cm and \(5\) cm respectively.
solution: Area of the sector \(= \dfrac{r}{2} \times \text{length of arc} = \dfrac{5}{2} \times 10 = 25\ \text{cm}^{2}\). Thus, the area of the sector is \(25\ \text{cm}^{2}\).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius \(4.2\) cm. \(\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\)
solution: Surface area of a sphere \(= 4\pi r^{2} = 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times (4.2)^{2} = 221.76\ \text{cm}^{2}\). Thus, the surface area of the sphere is \(221.76\ \text{cm}^{2}\).

stem: Adjacent sides of a parallelogram are \(11\) cm and \(17\) cm. If the length of one of its diagonals is \(26\) cm, find the length of the other.
solution: Let \(\square PQRS\) be the parallelogram with \(PQ = 17\) cm, \(QR = 11\) cm and diagonal \(PR = 26\) cm. The diagonals bisect each other at \(M\), so \(PM = MR = \dfrac{1}{2}PR = 13\) cm and \(QS = 2QM\). In \(\triangle PQR\), \(QM\) is the median, so by Apollonius theorem \(PQ^{2} + QR^{2} = 2PM^{2} + 2QM^{2}\). \(\therefore (17)^{2} + (11)^{2} = 2(13)^{2} + 2QM^{2}\). \(\therefore 289 + 121 = 2(169) + 2QM^{2}\), i.e. \(410 = 338 + 2QM^{2}\). Dividing by 2: \(205 = 169 + QM^{2}\), so \(QM^{2} = 36\) and \(QM = 6\). \(\therefore QS = 2QM = 12\) cm. Thus, the length of the other diagonal is \(12\) cm.

stem: In the figure, secants containing chords \(RS\) and \(PQ\) of a circle intersect each other at point \(A\) in the exterior of the circle. If \(m(\text{arc } PCR) = 26^\circ\) and \(m(\text{arc } QDS) = 48^\circ\), then find: (i) \(m\angle PQR\) (ii) \(m\angle SPQ\) (iii) \(m\angle RAQ\).
solution: By the Inscribed Angle Theorem: (i) \(\angle PQR = \dfrac{1}{2}\,m(\text{arc } PCR) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 26^\circ = 13^\circ\). (ii) \(\angle SPQ = \dfrac{1}{2}\,m(\text{arc } QDS) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 48^\circ = 24^\circ\). (iii) In \(\triangle AQR\), by the remote (exterior) interior angle theorem, \(\angle RAQ + \angle AQR = \angle SRQ\). But \(\angle SRQ = \angle SPQ\) (angles subtended by the same arc \(SQ\)) and \(\angle AQR = \angle PQR\) (\(A\text{-}P\text{-}Q\)). \(\therefore m\angle RAQ = m\angle SPQ - m\angle PQR = 24^\circ - 13^\circ = 11^\circ\).
figureNote: circle with two secants from an exterior point A, one through chord R-S, the other through chord P-Q; arcs PCR and QDS marked, p-02

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Draw a circle of radius \(3.5\) cm. Take any point \(K\) on it. Draw a tangent to the circle at \(K\) without using the centre of the circle.
solution: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle of radius \(3.5\) cm and take any point \(K\) on it. (2) Draw a chord \(KL\) through \(K\) and take any point \(M\) on the major arc \(KL\). (3) Join \(KM\) and \(ML\). (4) Construct \(\angle LKR\) congruent to the inscribed angle \(\angle KML\) (since \(\angle KML = \angle KLR\), tangent-chord angle). Extend the arm on both sides to obtain line \(PR\), the required tangent to the circle at \(K\).

stem: If \(\sec\alpha = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\), then find the value of \(\dfrac{1 - \csc\alpha}{1 + \csc\alpha}\), where \(\alpha\) is in the IV quadrant.
solution: \(\alpha\) is in quadrant IV, so \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\). \(\sec\alpha = \dfrac{r}{x} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\). Let \(r = 2k\), then \(x = \sqrt{3}\,k\). From \(r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}\): \((2k)^{2} = (\sqrt{3}k)^{2} + y^{2}\), so \(y^{2} = 4k^{2} - 3k^{2} = k^{2}\), giving \(y = \pm k\). Since \(y\) is negative, \(y = -k\). \(\therefore \csc\alpha = \dfrac{r}{y} = \dfrac{2k}{-k} = -2\). \(\therefore \dfrac{1 - \csc\alpha}{1 + \csc\alpha} = \dfrac{1 - (-2)}{1 + (-2)} = \dfrac{3}{-1} = -3\).

stem: Write the equation of the line passing through the pair of points \((2, 3)\) and \((4, 7)\) in the form \(y = mx + c\).
solution: Using \(\dfrac{y - y_1}{y_2 - y_1} = \dfrac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x_1}\) with \((x_1, y_1) = (2, 3)\) and \((x_2, y_2) = (4, 7)\): \(\dfrac{y - 3}{7 - 3} = \dfrac{x - 2}{4 - 2}\), i.e. \(\dfrac{y - 3}{4} = \dfrac{x - 2}{2}\). \(\therefore y - 3 = 2(x - 2) = 2x - 4\). \(\therefore y = 2x - 1\). The equation of the line is \(y = 2x - 1\).

stem: Prove that "The lengths of the two tangent segments to a circle drawn from an external point are equal."
solution: Given: A circle with centre \(O\) and an external point \(P\); \(PA\) and \(PB\) are the two tangents from \(P\) touching the circle at \(A\) and \(B\). To prove: \(PA = PB\). Construction: Draw seg \(OA\), seg \(OB\) and seg \(OP\). Proof: In \(\triangle OAP\) and \(\triangle OBP\): \(OA = OB\) (radii of the same circle); \(OP = OP\) (common side); \(\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ\) (tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact). \(\therefore \triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP\) (by R.H.S.). \(\therefore PA = PB\) (corresponding sides of congruent triangles). Hence, the lengths of the two tangent segments to a circle drawn from an external point are equal.

stem: A person standing on the bank of a river observes that the angle of elevation of the top of a tree standing on the opposite bank is \(60^\circ\). When he moves \(40\) m away from the bank, he finds the angle of elevation to be \(30^\circ\). Find the height of the tree and the width of the river. \((\sqrt{3} = 1.73)\)
solution: Let \(AB = h\) be the height of the tree, \(BC\) the width of the river, and let the person move from \(C\) to \(D\) with \(CD = 40\) m. In right \(\triangle ABC\): \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{BC} = \sqrt{3}\), so \(BC = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\). In right \(\triangle ABD\): \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{BD} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(BD = h\sqrt{3}\). Now \(BD - BC = 40\): \(h\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} = 40\), i.e. \(\dfrac{3h - h}{\sqrt{3}} = 40\), so \(2h = 40\sqrt{3}\), giving \(h = 20\sqrt{3}\) m. Then \(BC = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{20\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} = 20\) m. Thus, the height of the tree is \(20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6\) m and the width of the river is \(20\) m.

stem: \(A(5, 4)\), \(B(-3, -2)\) and \(C(1, -8)\) are the vertices of \(\triangle ABC\). Find the equations of median \(AD\) and the line parallel to \(AC\) passing through the point \(B\).
solution: \(D\) is the midpoint of \(BC\): \(D = \left(\dfrac{-3 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{-2 - 8}{2}\right) = (-1, -5)\). Slope of \(AD\) with \(A(5, 4)\), \(D(-1, -5)\): \(m = \dfrac{4 - (-5)}{5 - (-1)} = \dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). Using \(y = mx + c\) through \(A(5, 4)\): \(4 = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 5 + c\), so \(c = -\dfrac{7}{2}\). \(\therefore\) equation of median \(AD\) is \(y = \dfrac{3x}{2} - \dfrac{7}{2}\), i.e. \(2y = 3x - 7\). Slope of \(AC\) with \(A(5, 4)\), \(C(1, -8)\): \(m = \dfrac{-8 - 4}{1 - 5} = \dfrac{-12}{-4} = 3\). The line parallel to \(AC\) through \(B(-3, -2)\) has slope \(3\): \(-2 = 3(-3) + c\), so \(c = 7\). \(\therefore\) its equation is \(y = 3x + 7\).

stem: In the figure, \(AE = EF = AF = BE = CF = a\) and \(AT \perp BC\). Show that \(AB = AC = \sqrt{3}\,a\).
solution: \(\triangle AEF\) is equilateral (\(AE = EF = AF = a\)), and \(AT\) is its altitude, so \(ET = TF = \dfrac{a}{2}\) and \(BT = CT = a + \dfrac{a}{2}\). In right triangles \(\triangle ATB\) and \(\triangle ATC\): \(AT = AT\) (common); \(\angle ATB = \angle ATC = 90^\circ\); \(BT = CT\). \(\therefore \triangle ATB \cong \triangle ATC\) (SAS), so \(AB = AC\). Altitude of equilateral \(\triangle AEF\): \(AT = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a\). In \(\triangle ATB\): \(AB^{2} = AT^{2} + BT^{2} = \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a\right)^{2} + \left(a + \dfrac{a}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{3a^{2}}{4} + \dfrac{9a^{2}}{4} = \dfrac{12a^{2}}{4} = 3a^{2}\). \(\therefore AB = \sqrt{3}\,a\). Hence \(AB = AC = \sqrt{3}\,a\).
figureNote: isosceles triangle ABC with points E, T, F on base BC; AE = EF = AF = BE = CF = a and AT perpendicular to BC, p-03

stem: \(\triangle SHR \sim \triangle SVU\). In \(\triangle SHR\), \(SH = 4.5\) cm, \(HR = 5.2\) cm, \(SR = 5.8\) cm and \(\dfrac{SH}{SV} = \dfrac{3}{5}\). Construct \(\triangle SVU\).
solution: Steps of construction: (1) Construct \(\triangle SHR\) with \(SH = 4.5\) cm, \(SR = 5.8\) cm and \(HR = 5.2\) cm; extend \(SH\) and \(SR\). (2) Draw ray \(SX\) making an acute angle with \(SH\) on the side opposite to \(R\). (3) Since \(\dfrac{SH}{SV} = \dfrac{3}{5}\) and \(5 > 3\), locate points \(A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4, A_5\) on \(SX\) such that \(SA_1 = A_1A_2 = A_2A_3 = A_3A_4 = A_4A_5\). (4) Join \(A_3H\) and draw a line through \(A_5\) parallel to \(A_3H\), meeting the extended \(SH\) at \(V\). (5) Draw a line \(VU\) through \(V\) parallel to \(HR\), meeting the extended \(SR\) at \(U\). \(\triangle SVU\) is the required triangle.

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: Water flows at the rate of \(15\) m per minute through a cylindrical pipe having diameter \(20\) mm. How much time will it take to fill a conical vessel of base diameter \(40\) cm and depth \(45\) cm?
solution: Radius of the pipe \(= \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\) mm \(= 1\) cm; speed of water \(= 15\) m/min \(= 1500\) cm/min. Volume of water flowing per minute \(= \pi r^{2}h = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 1^{2} \times 1500 = \dfrac{33000}{7}\ \text{cm}^{3}\). Radius of the conical vessel \(= \dfrac{40}{2} = 20\) cm, depth \(= 45\) cm. Capacity of the cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 20 \times 20 \times 45 = \dfrac{396000}{21}\ \text{cm}^{3}\). Time required \(= \dfrac{\text{capacity of vessel}}{\text{volume flowing per minute}} = \dfrac{396000/21}{33000/7} = \dfrac{396}{99} = 4\) minutes. Thus, the time required to fill the conical vessel is \(4\) minutes.
